analysis.one_liner: Counts veterans' benefits as federal aid for-profit colleges must limit, protecting the GI Bill.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor or hearing, and the 90/10 rule still counts veterans' benefits as non-federal revenue.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires for-profit colleges to get at least 10% of revenue from non-federal sources, but the Post-9/11 GI Bill and other veterans' education benefits are not counted as federal money. That loophole lets schools that rely on veterans' tuition dollars still qualify for federal student aid. This bill would count veterans' benefits toward the federal share, so colleges that drew more than 90% of their money from federal sources, including veterans' benefits, would lose eligibility for federal student aid.
analysis.who_benefits: Veterans and service members using education benefits, who would be protected from schools that exist mainly to capture their GI Bill dollars, and taxpayers, who would stop subsidizing federal aid to schools that are almost entirely federally funded.

how_it_helps.text: Closes the loophole in the 90/10 rule by counting veterans' education benefits as federal revenue, so schools cannot use GI Bill money to game the federal-aid eligibility test.
Schools that failed the revised test would lose eligibility for federal student aid, reducing taxpayer spending on schools that derive nearly all revenue from federal programs.

analysis.who_pays: Proprietary (for-profit) colleges that depend heavily on veterans' education benefits and federal student aid for their revenue would bear the cost if they could not find other revenue sources.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges relying on federal money

drawbacks.text: Some for-profit colleges serving large numbers of veterans might lose federal aid eligibility, potentially disrupting enrolled students unless they could shift revenue sources or close to other institutions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A targeted fix to a specific loophole: it protects veterans and taxpayers at the expense of schools built on federal funding, though its practical impact depends on how many schools fail the revised test.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, where it sat until Congress ended without any further action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 16, 2011, and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training in March 2012.
No further action was taken before the 112th Congress ended.
The bill had no cosponsors during its life.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that draw heavily on veterans' benefits and federal student aid are better off, since the 90/10 rule was never changed and their federal funding flows continued unchanged. Veterans gained nothing because the bill never became law.

for.name: Mike Quigley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed closing the veterans' benefits loophole.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action, effectively killing it without a hearing or vote.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: Widely reported lobbying against 90/10 rule reforms during this period, though no direct action is documented in the bill record.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors from either party and no floor or committee votes, so no partisan pattern can be established from the record.

industries.note: Would lose access to federal student aid if veterans' benefits were counted toward the 90% federal revenue share, threatening schools dependent on GI Bill money. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the interests of veterans who might benefit from the change.
